claims.text: Conventional powder-metallurgical W–Cu composites typically contain phase separation and voids at W–Cu interfaces.
Tungsten particles can be conformally coated with a thin nickel layer by atomic layer deposition.
Spark-plasma sintering is a feasible powder-consolidation method.
The proposed W–Cu processing range is 1200–1600 °C in a controlled atmosphere.
The proposed 1200–1600 °C processing range is well below the boiling point of copper.
ALD will create a uniform nanoscale nickel layer covering the tungsten surfaces.
A nickel coating will improve wetting between tungsten and copper during consolidation.
A nickel coating will enhance interfacial diffusion between tungsten and copper during sintering.
The nickel interlayer will form a graded transition at the W–Cu interface.
The graded nickel-containing transition will accommodate thermal and irradiation-induced strains.
Improved wetting, diffusion, and strain accommodation will reduce interfacial void formation and phase separation.
Relative to direct SPS or infiltration without coating, ALD Ni-coated W–Cu will have a lower void fraction.
Relative to direct SPS or infiltration without coating, ALD Ni-coated W–Cu will have stronger interfacial bonding.
Relative to direct SPS or infiltration without coating, ALD Ni-coated W–Cu will have higher thermal conductivity.
Relative to direct SPS or infiltration without coating, ALD Ni-coated W–Cu will retain greater mechanical durability under operational and irradiation conditions.
Uncoated, vapor-coated, and mechanically alloyed W–Cu baselines still tend to contain phase-separated regions and voids that impair performance.
The expected benefit is limited to material thicknesses and irradiation doses typical of fusion-reactor joints.
The long-term stability of the nickel interlayer under high irradiation flux is unknown.
Nickel-interlayer thickness and thermal-expansion mismatch may affect the magnitude of the performance enhancement.
